posts.title: Prolotherapy for Shoulder Pain Relief: A Comprehensive Guide to Understanding Its Benefits and Effectiveness
posts.excerpt: Prolotherapy has become a common topic among patients researching options for shoulder pain that has not responded to rest or physical therapy alone. Here is a clear look at how it works and what to expect. The same regenerative approach applied to the knee is described in prolotherapy as a way to avoid knee surgery. […]
posts.content:
Prolotherapy has become a common topic among patients researching options for shoulder pain that has not responded to rest or physical therapy alone. Here is a clear look at how it works and what to expect. The same regenerative approach applied to the knee is described in prolotherapy as a way to avoid knee surgery.

What prolotherapy is

Prolotherapy involves injecting an irritant solution, often a dextrose solution, into the area around a damaged ligament or tendon. The goal is to trigger the body’s own repair response in that specific area.

Why it is used for shoulder pain

Shoulder pain frequently involves ligament or tendon laxity, particularly after an injury or with chronic overuse. Prolotherapy targets that specific tissue rather than simply masking the pain with medication. Shoulder pain that involves the rotator cuff is covered in rotator cuff and shoulder pain treatment.

What the treatment process looks like

Prolotherapy typically requires a series of injections spaced several weeks apart, rather than a single treatment. Some soreness at the injection site in the days following is common and generally temporary.

Understanding realistic expectations

Results vary by patient and by the severity of the underlying condition. Prolotherapy is not guaranteed to eliminate pain entirely, and is often used alongside other treatment such as physical therapy or drug-free options like Class IV laser therapy.

Is prolotherapy right for your shoulder pain

A thorough evaluation is the best way to determine whether prolotherapy fits your specific diagnosis, or whether a non-invasive option should be tried first.

Frequently asked questions

Which shoulder problems is prolotherapy least likely to help?
It is generally a poor fit for a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, a large labral tear, marked instability after a dislocation, or advanced shoulder arthritis, because those involve structural damage rather than simple ligament laxity. Frozen shoulder is also usually managed differently. An examination and imaging help separate a lax, irritated tendon from a tear that needs another approach.

Can prolotherapy be used after shoulder surgery that did not relieve the pain?
Sometimes, once healing is complete and the repair itself is intact. Pain that persists after shoulder surgery can come from scar tissue, altered mechanics, or nearby ligaments and tendons that were never the surgical target, and those are what prolotherapy aims at. A review of the operative report and current imaging comes first, since ongoing pain can also signal a failed repair.

Should shoulder physical therapy continue during a course of prolotherapy?
Usually yes, with the first few days after each injection kept gentle. Providers commonly ask patients to avoid heavy loading and aggressive stretching briefly, then resume strengthening, because the injection is meant to support tissue that still has to be trained to hold the shoulder stable. Stopping rehabilitation altogether tends to waste whatever the injections achieve.

How many prolotherapy sessions are tried before deciding it is not helping?
Most protocols use a series spaced a few weeks apart, and the decision point usually comes after three or four injections rather than after the first. If pain and shoulder function have not shifted at all by then, the sensible step is to revisit the diagnosis instead of continuing the series. The exact number varies with the condition being treated.

posts.title: Avoiding Surgery for Your Knee Pain: The Benefits of Prolotherapy
posts.excerpt: For patients with knee pain who want to explore options before considering surgery, prolotherapy is one non-surgical treatment worth understanding, particularly since it’s often confused with other injection-based therapies. The same approach applied to the shoulder is described in prolotherapy for shoulder pain. What Prolotherapy Actually Is Prolotherapy involves injecting a dextrose (sugar water) solution […]
posts.content:
For patients with knee pain who want to explore options before considering surgery, prolotherapy is one non-surgical treatment worth understanding, particularly since it’s often confused with other injection-based therapies. The same approach applied to the shoulder is described in prolotherapy for shoulder pain.

What Prolotherapy Actually Is

Prolotherapy involves injecting a dextrose (sugar water) solution into the area around a weakened or injured ligament or tendon. It’s a different treatment from platelet-rich plasma or stem cell injections, since it doesn’t use any blood-derived or biologic material. The theory is that the injection triggers a mild, localized inflammatory response that may prompt the body’s natural repair process in the treated tissue.

Who Might Consider It

Prolotherapy is typically considered for chronic knee pain related to ligament laxity or tendon irritation that hasn’t responded well to physical therapy or other conservative treatment, in patients looking to explore options before knee replacement surgery. It’s generally not a first-line treatment and works best after more established options have been tried.

What the Evidence Shows

Research on prolotherapy for knee osteoarthritis and ligament injuries is still developing, with some studies showing meaningful improvement in pain and function, and others showing more modest results. Because the evidence base is mixed, it’s best approached as one option among several rather than a guaranteed alternative to surgery. The equivalent decision-making for the knee is laid out in how to approach knee pain treatment.

What a Treatment Course Looks Like

Prolotherapy typically involves a series of injections spaced several weeks apart rather than a single visit. Sessions are generally well tolerated, with temporary soreness at the injection site being the most common and short-lived side effect. Individual results vary, and prolotherapy is not guaranteed to eliminate knee pain or avoid the need for surgery.

If you’re exploring non-surgical options for knee pain, a pain management provider can help you understand whether prolotherapy is a reasonable fit for your situation.

Frequently asked questions

Does trying prolotherapy first affect a knee replacement done later?
There is no evidence that it does. The solution is placed around soft tissue rather than into the joint surfaces, so it is not generally considered to complicate a later operation. Time is the bigger consideration: when a knee is already severely arthritic and function is declining month by month, a long delay can affect how well recovery from surgery goes.

Is prolotherapy worth trying for a bone-on-bone knee?
Usually not as a way to avoid replacement. Once imaging shows cartilage is largely gone, the pain is coming from the joint surface rather than from lax ligaments, which is what this treatment targets. Some providers still use it for painful ligaments or tendons around such a knee, but the realistic goal there is comfort, not a change in the joint itself.

Can prolotherapy help knee pain left over from an old ACL or MCL injury?
It is sometimes used for lingering tenderness or mild laxity around a healed ligament, particularly at the attachment points where it meets bone. It is not a substitute for reconstruction when a ligament is fully torn and the knee gives way under load. An examination that formally tests the knee for instability is what separates those two situations.

Can prolotherapy be used in a knee that also has a meniscus tear?
It may be considered when the tear is degenerative and the symptoms seem to come from surrounding ligament and tendon irritation. A knee that locks, catches, gives way or will not fully straighten points instead toward a mechanical problem that needs a surgical opinion first. Examination plus imaging is what separates those two pictures before any injection is planned.

posts.excerpt: New York City pain patients have more options today than they did even a few years ago. Here is a practical guide to finding relief through advanced, technology-based therapies. Moving past medication as the default For decades, medication was the first and sometimes only option offered to pain patients. Advanced therapies now give patients a […]
posts.content:
New York City pain patients have more options today than they did even a few years ago. Here is a practical guide to finding relief through advanced, technology-based therapies.

Moving past medication as the default

For decades, medication was the first and sometimes only option offered to pain patients. Advanced therapies now give patients a way to target the source of pain directly, without the risks that come with long-term medication use.

The core technologies changing pain care

Shockwave therapy (ESWT), EMTT, and Class IV laser therapy are three of the most established drug-free options currently available in New York City clinics, each targeting pain through a different mechanism, and often used together for a more complete treatment plan.

What makes a clinic worth choosing

Look for a provider who offers more than one of these technologies, takes time to evaluate your specific condition, and accepts your insurance, whether that is Medicaid, Healthfirst, Fidelis Care, or another major plan.

Finding relief close to home

Brooklyn residents do not need to travel across the city for advanced care. Pain management practices are located in neighborhoods including Williamsburg, Flatbush, and the Five Towns, which makes ongoing treatment easier to fit into daily life.

The right combination of technology, provider, and insurance access can make the difference between managing pain indefinitely and actually finding relief.

Frequently asked questions

Is it better to have shockwave, EMTT and laser at one clinic or separate providers?
One clinic is usually simpler, because these technologies are often sequenced within the same visit and adjusted together as a person responds. Splitting them across providers makes it harder to tell which is helping and can produce overlapping or conflicting plans. What matters most is that a single provider owns the diagnosis and the overall treatment schedule.

What should you ask a clinic before starting technology-based pain treatment?
Ask which conditions the device is being used for, how many sessions the plan calls for, who operates the equipment and what their training is, and how progress will be measured. It is also fair to ask what happens if nothing has changed partway through. A clear answer about that review point is a better sign than a confident promise of results.

Do advanced pain technologies replace physical therapy?
Generally no. They are typically used to reduce pain enough that rehabilitation becomes possible, and the strength and mobility work still has to be done. Most plans run the two alongside each other, progressing exercise as symptoms settle. Skipping the rehabilitation portion is a common reason gains fade once a course of treatment finishes.

How many visits a week do technology-based pain treatments usually require?
Most protocols involve one or two visits a week across several weeks, with each appointment lasting a short time. That cadence is worth weighing when choosing a provider, since a schedule that cannot realistically be kept is unlikely to help. Some clinics group more than one technology into a single appointment specifically to cut down the number of trips.

posts.excerpt: Pain management in New York has evolved into a more comprehensive practice than it once was, combining technology, insurance access, and patient-centered care into a single approach. Here is what that looks like. Starting with a real evaluation Comprehensive pain management begins with a full evaluation of a patient’s condition and history, not just the […]
posts.content:
Pain management in New York has evolved into a more comprehensive practice than it once was, combining technology, insurance access, and patient-centered care into a single approach. Here is what that looks like.

Starting with a real evaluation

Comprehensive pain management begins with a full evaluation of a patient’s condition and history, not just the symptom that brought them into the office that day. This helps a provider build a plan targeted at the actual source of the pain.

Combining drug-free technology and traditional care

Rather than choosing one path, a comprehensive approach often blends drug-free options like shockwave therapy, EMTT, and Class IV laser therapy with traditional care when appropriate, giving each patient more than one tool to work with.

Making advanced care accessible

A comprehensive approach also means accessible care. Accepting a broad range of insurance, including Medicaid, Healthfirst, Fidelis Care, MetroPlus, Affinity Health Plan, Amerigroup, and BlueCross BlueShield, ensures more patients can actually use the care available to them.

Building a plan around the whole patient

Chronic pain affects sleep, mood, and daily function, not just the physical symptom. A comprehensive plan considers all of it, adjusting over time as a patient’s condition and goals change.

Brooklyn clinics that bring this comprehensive approach together serve patients across the borough’s diverse communities.

Frequently asked questions

Does treating sleep and mood really change chronic pain?
It can. Poor sleep lowers pain tolerance and low mood tends to reduce activity, and both feed back into the pain itself. Addressing them is not a suggestion that the pain is imagined; it is treating factors that make the same physical problem hurt more and recover more slowly. Many plans build sleep and stress strategies in alongside physical treatment.

Does pain medication have to be stopped before starting a comprehensive plan?
Usually not at the start. Medication is commonly continued while other treatment is introduced, then reviewed as symptoms change, and any reduction is normally gradual and planned with the prescriber. Stopping abruptly without guidance can cause a rebound in pain or withdrawal effects, depending on the drug, so it is not something to attempt alone.

Can one treatment plan cover pain in more than one part of the body?
Yes, and that situation is common. Pain in several areas can reflect one underlying problem, a compensation pattern from favoring an injured side, or a more widespread pain condition, and each calls for a different plan. Providers generally prioritize whichever area is limiting function most, then reassess whether the others settle once that one improves.

Does a pain management plan include guidance about returning to work?
Often, at least as activity guidance and documentation. Plans commonly address lifting limits, sitting and standing tolerance, and a graded return to normal duties, and a provider can put restrictions in writing when an employer or insurer requires them. Physical or occupational therapists are sometimes brought in when the job has specific physical demands.

posts.excerpt: Pulsed Electromagnetic Field therapy, commonly known as PEMF, has been used for years to support bone and tissue healing. Here is an overview of how it works and where it fits among today’s pain management options. How it is being used locally is described in how EMTT therapy is changing pain management in Brooklyn. What […]
posts.content:
Pulsed Electromagnetic Field therapy, commonly known as PEMF, has been used for years to support bone and tissue healing. Here is an overview of how it works and where it fits among today’s pain management options. How it is being used locally is described in how EMTT therapy is changing pain management in Brooklyn.

What PEMF therapy is

PEMF uses low-frequency electromagnetic fields delivered to the body to potentially support cellular repair processes. It is a non-invasive, drug-free option that has been studied for its role in bone healing and tissue recovery.

How it may support healing

PEMF is thought to work at the cellular level, potentially encouraging the body’s natural regenerative processes in bone and soft tissue. It does not involve needles, incisions, or medication.

Where PEMF differs from EMTT

PEMF and EMTT are related but distinct technologies. EMTT uses higher-intensity electromagnetic energy and is generally used to target more acute inflammation and tissue repair, while PEMF has traditionally been studied more for lower-intensity, longer-term applications like bone healing.

Discussing your options with a provider

Whether PEMF, EMTT, shockwave therapy, or Class IV laser therapy is the right fit depends on the specific condition being treated. A pain management evaluation can help determine which drug-free technology matches your needs.

If you are exploring non-invasive options for bone or tissue healing, a conversation with your provider can clarify which technology is appropriate for your specific case.

Frequently asked questions

Are home PEMF mats the same as clinical PEMF devices?
They are not equivalent. Consumer mats generally deliver far lower field intensity than clinical systems and are marketed for general wellness rather than a specific diagnosis. That does not make them harmful, but expecting a home mat to match a supervised device aimed at a defined target is unrealistic, and the claims made for consumer products vary widely in quality.

Can a home PEMF mat interfere with an implanted device?
Yes, that is the main reason implanted electronic devices are a contraindication for consumer magnetic mats as well as clinical equipment. A pulsed magnetic field can disturb a pacemaker, defibrillator, neurostimulator or programmable pump regardless of the device’s power. Anyone with an implant should clear any magnetic therapy, bought or clinical, with the clinician who manages it before use.

Can PEMF help a fracture that is not healing?
Bone stimulation is among the longest-studied uses of electromagnetic therapy, and it is sometimes considered for slow-healing or non-united fractures. It is used as an addition to orthopedic management rather than in place of it, and suitability depends on the fracture pattern, the fixation and why healing has stalled. An orthopedic assessment should come first.

What does a PEMF session feel like compared with EMTT?
Both are usually painless, and neither involves needles, incisions or heat at the skin. Higher-intensity electromagnetic treatment can produce a faint tapping or small muscle twitch in the treated area, while lower-intensity fields are frequently felt as nothing at all. Clothing generally stays on for both, and people typically return to ordinary activity immediately afterwards.

posts.title: Using shockwave treatment to avoid surgery and steroid injections
posts.excerpt: For patients weighing whether to move forward with surgery or steroid injections, shockwave therapy is worth understanding as a non-surgical option that’s often tried earlier in the treatment process. Why Patients Look for Alternatives First Surgery carries recovery time, risk, and cost, and repeated steroid injections come with their own limitations, including a cap on […]
posts.content:
For patients weighing whether to move forward with surgery or steroid injections, shockwave therapy is worth understanding as a non-surgical option that’s often tried earlier in the treatment process.

Why Patients Look for Alternatives First

Surgery carries recovery time, risk, and cost, and repeated steroid injections come with their own limitations, including a cap on how often they can safely be used in the same area. For chronic tendon and soft tissue conditions that haven’t responded to rest and physical therapy alone, shockwave therapy is often tried as a non-surgical option before more invasive steps.

How It Works

Shockwave therapy delivers acoustic pressure waves to the affected tissue, which may help stimulate blood flow and the body’s natural healing response in chronically irritated tendons and connective tissue. It’s most commonly used for conditions like plantar fasciitis, tendinitis, and other soft tissue injuries that have become chronic.

What the Research Suggests

Studies suggest shockwave therapy can lead to meaningful improvement for certain chronic tendon conditions, though results vary by condition and by patient. It’s generally viewed as a reasonable option to try before surgery, though it isn’t a guaranteed alternative and doesn’t work for every case.

What a Treatment Course Involves

Shockwave therapy typically requires a series of sessions rather than a single treatment, spaced about a week apart. Sessions are generally well tolerated, with some mild soreness during and shortly after treatment being the most common and short-lived side effect. Individual results vary, and shockwave therapy is not guaranteed to eliminate the need for surgery or injections.

If you’re weighing your options before surgery or another round of steroid injections, a pain management provider can help you understand whether shockwave therapy makes sense to try first.

Frequently asked questions

How long after a cortisone injection can shockwave therapy be started?
Many providers wait several weeks after a steroid injection before beginning shockwave, so the intended tissue response is not blunted and so it stays clear which treatment is responsible for any change. The interval varies with the site and with how many injections have been given. Reporting the date of the last injection matters more than any fixed waiting period.

Does trying shockwave first delay surgery if surgery turns out to be needed?
A course usually runs a few weeks, which is short relative to the wait for most elective procedures, and shockwave does not alter tissue in a way that complicates a later operation. Timing does matter for problems such as a complete tendon rupture or nerve compression with weakness, where delay can affect the surgical result, so those need assessment first.

Is shockwave therapy the same as the ultrasound used in physical therapy?
No. Therapeutic ultrasound delivers continuous sound energy mainly to warm tissue, while shockwave delivers short, high-pressure acoustic pulses intended to provoke a repair response in chronically irritated tissue. The sensation differs as well: shockwave is felt as sharp tapping and can be briefly uncomfortable, whereas therapeutic ultrasound is usually barely noticeable.

Can a course of shockwave therapy be repeated if the pain comes back?
Usually yes. Repeat courses are common for chronic tendon problems that flare again with a return to heavy activity, and there is no lifetime cap of the kind that applies to repeated steroid injections in one area. A provider would normally reexamine first, since returning pain can mean the load or technique driving the problem has not been addressed.

posts.title: How common is chronic pain and how pain management can help you?
posts.excerpt: Chronic pain is far more common than most people realize, and it affects nearly every part of daily life when left unmanaged. Here is what patients should understand about it, and how professional pain management can help. How common is chronic pain, really Chronic pain, generally defined as pain lasting more than three months, affects […]
posts.content:
Chronic pain is far more common than most people realize, and it affects nearly every part of daily life when left unmanaged. Here is what patients should understand about it, and how professional pain management can help.

How common is chronic pain, really

Chronic pain, generally defined as pain lasting more than three months, affects a significant share of adults, and rates tend to increase with age. It is one of the leading reasons people seek ongoing medical care.

Why chronic pain is different from an injury

An acute injury has a clear starting point and typically heals within weeks. Chronic pain often continues long after the original cause has healed, or exists without a single identifiable injury, which makes it harder to treat with a one-time fix.

How pain management addresses it differently

Rather than treating a single flare-up, pain management builds a plan around the patient’s specific condition, which may include drug-free technology such as shockwave therapy, EMTT, and Class IV laser therapy, alongside lifestyle and activity guidance.

The cost of leaving it untreated

Untreated chronic pain does not just affect the body. It can impact sleep, mood, work, and relationships over time, which is why an early, professional evaluation tends to lead to better long-term outcomes.

If pain has become a constant part of your daily life, a pain management evaluation is the first step toward a plan built around your specific condition, with broad insurance access including Medicaid.

Frequently asked questions

Can chronic pain be real when scans and blood tests come back normal?
Yes. Many chronic pain conditions involve changes in how nerves and the nervous system process signals, and those changes do not show on an X-ray, MRI or blood panel. Normal results are useful because they rule out certain structural causes, but they do not mean nothing is wrong, and they do not mean treatment will not help.

Does chronic pain get worse if it is left untreated for years?
It tends to become harder to treat rather than simply more intense. Long-standing pain usually brings reduced activity, muscle deconditioning and disrupted sleep, and the nervous system can grow more sensitive over time, so the original problem ends up sitting inside a larger pattern. That does not make late treatment pointless, but it often takes longer to unwind.

Is chronic pain only a problem for older adults?
No. Rates do rise with age, but younger adults develop chronic pain after injuries, from repetitive demands at work or in sport, and from conditions such as migraine, back pain and inflammatory disease. Age shifts which causes are most likely rather than whether persistent pain deserves a proper evaluation in the first place.

Does pain that comes and goes still count as chronic pain?
Generally yes. Pain that recurs across more than about three months is usually classed as chronic even when there are comfortable stretches in between, which is how back pain and migraine often behave. What matters clinically is the pattern over months, so a simple record of how often flares occur and what triggers them is useful at an evaluation.

posts.excerpt: The title “pain management doctor” covers a broad range of responsibilities, and understanding what they actually do can help patients know what to expect from their care. Diagnosing the source of pain A pain management doctor’s first job is identifying what is actually causing a patient’s pain, whether that is a joint condition, nerve irritation, […]
posts.content:
The title “pain management doctor” covers a broad range of responsibilities, and understanding what they actually do can help patients know what to expect from their care.

Diagnosing the source of pain

A pain management doctor’s first job is identifying what is actually causing a patient’s pain, whether that is a joint condition, nerve irritation, an old injury, or a combination of factors.

Building a personalized treatment plan

Once a diagnosis is clear, the doctor builds a treatment plan specific to that patient, which may include drug-free technology such as shockwave therapy, EMTT, and Class IV laser therapy, physical therapy, or interventional procedures when appropriate.

Coordinating care across specialists

Pain management doctors often coordinate with other providers, including physical therapists, surgeons, and primary care physicians, to make sure a patient’s overall care plan works together rather than in isolation.

Adjusting treatment over time

Chronic pain conditions change, and so should treatment plans. A pain management doctor monitors progress and adjusts the approach as a patient responds, rather than sticking rigidly to an initial plan.

Helping patients navigate insurance

Part of the role also includes helping patients understand what their insurance, including Medicaid, Healthfirst, Fidelis Care, or MetroPlus, actually covers, so cost does not become a barrier to effective treatment.

A good pain management doctor treats the diagnosis, not just the symptom, and stays involved throughout the entire course of a patient’s care.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a pain management doctor and an orthopedic surgeon?
An orthopedic surgeon focuses on structural problems that may require an operation, while a pain management physician concentrates on diagnosing and treating pain without surgery, using medication, image-guided procedures, therapy and technology-based options. The two frequently share patients, with the pain physician managing ongoing symptoms and the surgeon consulted when a structural repair is genuinely on the table.

Do pain management doctors prescribe opioids?
Some do, within monitoring and clear limits, but current practice treats opioids as one narrow part of a plan rather than the default. Many pain physicians work mainly through procedures, non-opioid medication and rehabilitation. A practice that leads with long-term opioid prescribing before establishing a diagnosis and a broader plan is not following accepted standards.

Do pain management doctors perform surgery?
Generally no. Their procedures are interventional rather than surgical, including guided injections, nerve blocks and ablation techniques, usually performed in a clinic or procedure room with the patient going home the same day. When an operation is genuinely indicated, the pain physician refers to a surgeon and often keeps managing symptoms alongside that care.

Which doctor should be seen first for pain that will not go away?
A primary care physician is a reasonable starting point when pain is new or unexplained, since the cause may turn out to be straightforward. Pain that has persisted for months, resisted basic treatment, or already been investigated without producing a clear plan is where a pain specialist adds the most. Either route can lead to the same specialists eventually.

posts.title: How to Find the Best Pain Management Doctor in Brooklyn
posts.excerpt: TL;DR The right pain management doctor finds the cause of your pain, offers more than one way to treat it, and explains the plan clearly. Check board certification and training in pain medicine or a related specialty. Look for a range of treatment options, not a single procedure for everyone. Confirm insurance, location, hours and […]
posts.content:
TL;DR

The right pain management doctor finds the cause of your pain, offers more than one way to treat it, and explains the plan clearly.

  • Check board certification and training in pain medicine or a related specialty.
  • Look for a range of treatment options, not a single procedure for everyone.
  • Confirm insurance, location, hours and how easy it is to reach the office.
  • Be cautious of guaranteed results, pressure to commit to long packages, or opioid-only plans.

What does a pain management doctor do?

A pain management doctor diagnoses the source of ongoing pain and builds a treatment plan. Plans can include physical therapy, medication, injections, device-based therapies and lifestyle changes. They often coordinate with your primary care doctor and other specialists. See what a pain management doctor does.

What credentials should you look for?

  • Board certification in pain medicine, or in a related specialty such as physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R), anesthesiology or neurology, often with fellowship training in pain management.
  • A medical degree: MD (Doctor of Medicine) or DO (Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine). Both are fully licensed physicians.
  • A valid New York license, which you can check on the New York State Office of the Professions website.

What treatment options should a good practice offer?

Chronic pain rarely has a single fix. A strong practice can offer or coordinate several approaches:

  • Physical and occupational therapy
  • Image-guided injections when appropriate
  • Non-drug device-based therapies, such as shockwave or laser therapy
  • Medication management that limits long-term opioid use
  • Referral to surgeons or other specialists when needed

A practice with fewer tools that explains its limits and refers when needed can serve you better than one that offers everything and gives everyone the same plan.

How should the doctor approach diagnosis?

  • A detailed history: where it hurts, how long, what makes it better or worse
  • A hands-on physical exam
  • A review of earlier imaging and treatments
  • New tests only when they will change the plan
  • A clear explanation of the likely cause and the reasoning behind the plan

What practical things matter?

  • Your insurance is accepted, checked before your first visit
  • A location you can reach for follow-up visits
  • Hours that fit your schedule
  • Easy contact by phone or online
  • Reasonable wait times for a first appointment

What are the red flags?

  • Promises of a guaranteed cure
  • Pressure to buy large packages of sessions up front
  • The same treatment recommended for every patient
  • A plan built mainly around long-term opioids
  • Little time spent on your history or exam

What questions should you ask at the first visit?

  • What do you think is causing my pain?
  • What are my options, including non-drug options?
  • What results are realistic, and how long will it take?
  • What will my insurance cover, and what will I pay?
  • When should I expect to see improvement, and what happens if I do not?

See how pain management clinics work, pain management in Brooklyn and chronic pain.

Frequently asked questions

What kind of doctor is best for chronic pain?

A physician board certified in pain medicine or a related specialty such as physical medicine and rehabilitation or anesthesiology, who looks for the cause and offers several treatment options.

Is a DO as qualified as an MD for pain management?

Yes. Both are fully licensed physicians who complete residency and can train and certify in pain medicine.

Do I need a referral to see a pain management doctor?

Not with Original Medicare or many PPO plans. Many HMO, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans require one.

How do I know if a pain clinic is good?

Look for board-certified doctors, a clear diagnosis, a range of options, honest timelines and no pressure to commit to large packages.

What should I bring to my first pain management visit?

Your ID and insurance card, a list of medications, earlier imaging or reports, and notes on what has and has not helped.

Take the next step

If this sounds like what you are dealing with, you do not have to figure it out alone. A pain management provider can evaluate what is going on and walk you through drug-free, non-surgical options that may fit your situation.

Ready to get real relief?

We verify your coverage before your visit and build a non-surgical plan that fits you.

posts.excerpt: TL;DR Yes, in most cases. Medicare and Medicaid both cover pain management that is medically necessary, but the details depend on your plan and the treatment. Medicare Part B covers most outpatient pain care, such as doctor visits, physical therapy and many injections. Medicaid in New York covers medically necessary pain care, usually through a […]
posts.content:
If chronic pain is affecting your daily life, cost shouldn’t be the reason you put off getting care. One of the most common questions we hear from new patients in Brooklyn is whether Medicare or Medicaid will cover pain management treatment. The short answer is that both programs generally cover medically necessary pain management, but the specifics depend on your plan and the type of treatment.

What Medicare Typically Covers

Medicare Part B generally covers outpatient services that are considered medically necessary, which can include evaluation and management visits, certain diagnostic testing, and a range of treatments for chronic pain when ordered by a physician. Coverage details, including copays and whether prior authorization is needed, can vary depending on whether you have Original Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan, so it’s worth confirming specifics with your plan directly.

What Medicaid Typically Covers

Medicaid coverage for pain management varies more than Medicare, since Medicaid is administered at the state level and each state sets its own covered services and requirements. In New York, Medicaid generally covers medically necessary outpatient treatment for chronic pain conditions, though certain specialized or newer modalities may require prior authorization or may not be covered at all. A significant portion of the patients we see in our Brooklyn clinic carry Medicaid coverage. We accept Healthfirst, Fidelis Care, MetroPlus, Affinity Health Plan, Amerigroup, and BlueCross BlueShield, among other plans, and our front desk team works with patients regularly to sort out what’s covered before treatment starts.

Treatments That May Not Be Covered

Not every pain management option is covered by every plan. Some newer or more specialized treatments, certain injectable therapies, and elective or cosmetic-adjacent procedures may fall outside standard coverage, even when the underlying condition is covered. This is why it’s important to ask about coverage for a specific treatment before it’s scheduled, rather than assuming.

How to Check Your Benefits

The most reliable way to know what’s covered is to call the number on the back of your insurance card and ask specifically about pain management services, or to ask our office to help verify your benefits before your visit. Bringing your insurance card to your first appointment lets our team confirm coverage and walk you through any costs up front.

If you have Medicare or Medicaid and are dealing with chronic pain, our Brooklyn office can help you understand your coverage before your first visit. Request a callback and we’ll verify your benefits and get you scheduled.

posts.title: Cold Laser Therapy for Pain: How It Works and What It Treats
posts.excerpt: TL;DR Cold laser therapy, also called low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, uses low-power light to reduce pain and inflammation and support tissue healing. It does not cut or burn the skin. It is used for joint, tendon, muscle and nerve pain, including knee arthritis, neck and back pain and tendinitis. Sessions are short and usually […]
posts.content:
TL;DR

Cold laser therapy, also called low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, uses low-power light to reduce pain and inflammation and support tissue healing. It does not cut or burn the skin.

  • It is used for joint, tendon, muscle and nerve pain, including knee arthritis, neck and back pain and tendinitis.
  • Sessions are short and usually painless. Most courses run several sessions.
  • Research supports it for some conditions, and results vary from person to person.
  • It works best as part of a plan that includes movement and exercise.

What is cold laser therapy?

Cold laser therapy uses specific wavelengths of red and near-infrared light at low power. Unlike surgical lasers, it does not heat or cut tissue, which is why it is called “cold”. The light passes through the skin and is absorbed by cells in the treated area. It is also known as low-level laser therapy (LLLT) and photobiomodulation (PBM).

How does cold laser therapy work?

The light is absorbed by mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of cells. Research suggests this can:

  • Increase cell energy production
  • Reduce inflammation
  • Improve local blood flow
  • Calm pain signaling in nerves

The effect depends on the dose, the wavelength and how deep the target tissue is.

What conditions does cold laser therapy treat?

  • Knee osteoarthritis and other joint pain
  • Neck pain and low back pain
  • Tendinitis and tendinopathy, such as tennis elbow and Achilles pain
  • Plantar fasciitis
  • Peripheral neuropathy symptoms
  • Jaw pain (TMJ)
  • Muscle strains and sports injuries

See laser therapy for neuropathic pain and knee osteoarthritis treatment.

What does the evidence say?

Reviews of randomized trials have found that low-level laser therapy can reduce pain and improve function in knee osteoarthritis and chronic neck pain when the correct dose is used. Results in other conditions are more mixed. Laser therapy is usually one part of a plan rather than a stand-alone cure.

What does a session feel like?

  • You sit or lie comfortably while the handheld device is placed over the area.
  • Most people feel nothing, or mild warmth.
  • Sessions usually take 5 to 15 minutes.
  • Eye protection is worn.
  • You can return to normal activity right away.

Many people need several sessions over a few weeks before judging the result.

Who should avoid cold laser therapy?

Laser therapy is generally safe, but it is usually not used:

  • Directly over the eyes
  • Over a known or suspected cancer
  • Over the abdomen or low back during pregnancy
  • Over areas with recent steroid injections or active bleeding, in some cases

Tell the provider about your medical history before starting.

How is it different from high-intensity laser therapy?

High-intensity laser therapy uses more power to reach deeper tissue and often produces noticeable warmth. Cold laser uses lower power. Both are types of photobiomodulation. Learn more in our in-depth look at laser therapy for pain and about our laser therapy.

Frequently asked questions

Does cold laser therapy work for pain?

Research supports it for some conditions, such as knee osteoarthritis and neck pain, when the right dose is used. Results vary.

Is cold laser therapy painful?

No. Most people feel nothing or mild warmth.

How many cold laser sessions will I need?

Many people need several sessions over a few weeks. The number depends on the condition.

Is cold laser therapy safe?

It is generally safe when used correctly. Eye protection is worn, and it is avoided over certain areas.

Are home red light devices the same as cold laser therapy?

They share a principle, but clinical devices deliver a focused, controlled dose to a specific target. A home panel is not a direct substitute.

Take the next step

If this sounds like what you are dealing with, you do not have to figure it out alone. A pain management provider can evaluate what is going on and walk you through drug-free, non-surgical options that may fit your situation.

Ready to get real relief?

We verify your coverage before your visit and build a non-surgical plan that fits you.

posts.excerpt: Understanding what actually happens at a pain management clinic can make that first appointment feel far less intimidating. The initial evaluation Your first visit typically starts with a detailed conversation about your pain history, what treatments you have already tried, and what your goals are. […]
posts.content:
Understanding what actually happens at a pain management clinic can make that first appointment feel far less intimidating. Here is a straightforward walkthrough of how these clinics work.

The initial evaluation

Your first visit typically starts with a detailed conversation about your pain history, what treatments you have already tried, and what your goals are. This often includes a physical exam and may include imaging or lab work if needed.

Building a personalized treatment plan

Based on that evaluation, your provider builds a plan specific to your condition. This may include drug-free technology such as shockwave therapy, EMTT, or Class IV laser therapy, physical therapy, or in some cases, interventional procedures like guided injections.

How treatment sessions are structured

Most drug-free treatments involve a series of sessions over several weeks rather than a single visit. Your provider tracks your progress and adjusts the plan as needed based on how you respond.

Working with your insurance

A good pain management clinic will help verify what your insurance covers before starting treatment, so there are no surprises. Plans such as Healthfirst, Fidelis Care, MetroPlus, Affinity Health Plan, Amerigroup, BlueCross BlueShield, Medicaid, and Medicare are commonly accepted in Brooklyn.

Knowing what to expect ahead of time makes it easier to take that first step toward addressing pain that has been left untreated for too long.

Frequently asked questions

What happens if a pain treatment plan is not working halfway through?
The usual step is a reassessment rather than simply continuing the schedule. That can mean revisiting the diagnosis, ordering imaging that was not needed at first, changing the modality, or adding rehabilitation. A plan built on an assumption about the pain source is worth questioning as soon as the response is not what was expected, and asking for that review is reasonable.

Do you see the same provider at every pain clinic visit?
Often the physician handles evaluations and procedures while trained clinical staff deliver repeat treatment sessions under that physician’s plan, which is normal and keeps appointments efficient. What should stay constant is who is responsible for the plan overall, so it is worth knowing who reviews progress and who to contact if symptoms change between visits.

Is a patient expected to do anything between pain clinic sessions?
Usually yes. Most plans include home exercise, activity limits or pacing, and sometimes a simple pain and activity log, with the in-clinic sessions built around that work rather than replacing it. Skipping the home portion is one of the more common reasons a course delivers less than expected, so written instructions are worth asking for.

What happens once a course of pain treatment is finished?
Many plans close with a review, a maintenance exercise program, and guidance on which activities to reintroduce and at what pace. Some conditions are given a planned check-in several months later, particularly when the pain is tied to work or sport. There is normally a route back for a flare without repeating the entire initial evaluation.

posts.excerpt: Not knowing what to expect at a first pain clinic appointment keeps many patients from booking one in the first place. Here is a clear walkthrough of what actually happens. Before your appointment You will typically be asked to bring a list of current medications, any relevant imaging or test results, and a summary of […]
posts.content:
Not knowing what to expect at a first pain clinic appointment keeps many patients from booking one in the first place. Here is a clear walkthrough of what actually happens.

Before your appointment

You will typically be asked to bring a list of current medications, any relevant imaging or test results, and a summary of your pain history, including when it started and what has been tried so far.

The evaluation itself

Your provider will ask detailed questions about your pain and conduct a physical exam. This is the point where a proper diagnosis starts to take shape, rather than treatment being guessed at.

Discussing your treatment options

Once your provider understands your condition, they will walk through the treatment options available, which may include drug-free technology such as shockwave therapy, EMTT, or Class IV laser therapy, along with any other relevant options.

Insurance and scheduling

Before you leave, staff will typically confirm what your insurance, whether Medicaid, Healthfirst, Fidelis Care, or another plan, covers, and help schedule any follow-up sessions your plan requires.

What to expect after your first visit

Most treatment plans involve a series of sessions rather than a single appointment. Your provider will track your progress and adjust the plan as needed based on how you respond.

Knowing what to expect ahead of time makes that first appointment far less intimidating, and often the hardest part is simply making the call to schedule it.

Frequently asked questions

Does treatment usually start at the first pain clinic appointment?
Sometimes. When the diagnosis is already clear and no further testing is needed, a first treatment session can happen the same day. More often the visit ends with a plan and a scheduled start, especially if imaging, blood work or plan approval is required first. Asking when booking makes it easier to plan around the appointment.

How should pain be described so the evaluation is accurate?
Specifics help far more than a number alone. Where the pain starts and whether it travels, what makes it better or worse, how it behaves across a day, whether there is numbness, tingling or weakness, and which activities it now prevents all point toward a cause. A few days of notes beforehand is more reliable than recalling everything on the spot.

What if there are no scans or old records to bring to the appointment?
It is not a problem. History and physical examination direct the workup, and imaging is ordered when it would actually change the plan rather than as a routine first step. If scans were done elsewhere, the images themselves are more useful than the written report, and most facilities will release them on request, though it can take a few days.

Can a family member or interpreter come to a pain clinic appointment?
Yes, and it is often helpful, particularly when a long history has to be covered or several treatment options are being weighed. Interpretation in a medical setting is a patient right and is better arranged in advance than improvised. A second person can also write down the instructions given at the end, which are easy to forget afterwards.

posts.title: Ultrasound-Guided Injections For Pain In Brooklyn, New York
posts.excerpt: Ultrasound-guided injections are one of the more precise interventional tools available to Brooklyn pain patients. Here is a clear look at how the technique works. What ultrasound guidance adds Ultrasound imaging allows a physician to see soft tissue, joints, and nearby structures in real time while positioning a needle, improving accuracy compared to an injection […]
posts.content:
Ultrasound-guided injections are one of the more precise interventional tools available to Brooklyn pain patients. Here is a clear look at how the technique works.

What ultrasound guidance adds

Ultrasound imaging allows a physician to see soft tissue, joints, and nearby structures in real time while positioning a needle, improving accuracy compared to an injection done without imaging guidance.

Conditions this technique is used for

Ultrasound-guided injections are commonly used for joint pain, tendon injuries, and soft tissue conditions where precise placement of medication can meaningfully affect the outcome.

What the procedure involves

The procedure is done in a clinical setting using a handheld ultrasound probe alongside the injection. Most patients tolerate the procedure well and are able to resume normal activity soon after, with some soreness at the site being common.

How this compares to other guided techniques

Unlike fluoroscopy, ultrasound guidance does not use radiation, which makes it a preferred option for certain soft tissue targets and for patients where radiation exposure is a consideration. How image guidance is applied to pain procedures is set out in fluoroscopic guided injection for pain management.

Discussing whether it fits your condition

A pain management specialist can evaluate whether an ultrasound-guided injection, a drug-free option like shockwave or laser therapy, or a combination of approaches best fits your specific diagnosis.

Frequently asked questions

Does an ultrasound-guided injection hurt more than a regular injection?
Generally not. The probe rests on the skin and adds pressure rather than pain, and accurate placement can mean less searching with the needle than an unguided injection requires. Local anesthetic is typically used first. Some targets, such as a tight tendon sheath or a joint already under pressure, are uncomfortable regardless of how the needle is guided.

Is sedation used for these injections, and can you drive home afterwards?
Most ultrasound-guided injections are done with local anesthetic only, and driving afterwards is usually fine. Sedation is uncommon for this type of procedure. The exception is an injection whose numbing effect temporarily weakens a limb or makes a joint feel unsteady, in which case waiting for normal sensation to return is safer. The office will say in advance if arrangements are needed.

Which areas of the body cannot be reached with ultrasound guidance?
Ultrasound cannot see through bone, so deep spinal targets such as epidural and facet injections are normally done with fluoroscopy or CT instead. Very deep structures can also be difficult to image clearly in larger patients. The technique is strongest for joints, tendons, bursae and nerves that lie within range of the probe.

Why can pain increase for a day or two after a guided injection?
A short flare is common and usually reflects the volume of fluid placed into a confined space, irritation from the needle, or local anesthetic wearing off before the injected medication takes effect. It typically settles within a couple of days with relative rest and ice. Escalating pain with fever, spreading redness or swelling is different and should be reported promptly.

Unsure whether an injection is the right next step?

posts.excerpt: Cryotherapy has grown from an athletic recovery tool into a mainstream option for chronic pain management. Here is what it involves and how it may help Brooklyn patients dealing with ongoing pain. How it applies to chronic pain is covered in cryotherapy for chronic pain relief. What cryotherapy actually is Cryotherapy exposes the body, or […]
posts.content:
Cryotherapy has grown from an athletic recovery tool into a mainstream option for chronic pain management. Here is what it involves and how it may help Brooklyn patients dealing with ongoing pain. How it applies to chronic pain is covered in cryotherapy for chronic pain relief.

What cryotherapy actually is

Cryotherapy exposes the body, or a specific area of the body, to very cold temperatures for a short period of time. The goal is to trigger the body’s natural response to cold, which may help reduce inflammation and support recovery.

How it may help with pain

Many patients report a possible reduction in swelling and discomfort after cryotherapy sessions, particularly for joint and soft tissue pain. It is often used alongside other treatments rather than as a stand-alone solution.

What a typical session looks like

Sessions are generally brief, often lasting just a few minutes, and are done under supervision. Patients typically feel a noticeable cooling sensation followed by warmth as circulation returns to the treated area afterward.

Who might consider cryotherapy

Patients managing arthritis, muscle soreness, or inflammation-related pain sometimes look to cryotherapy as a complement to their broader treatment plan, which may include drug-free technology like shockwave therapy or Class IV laser therapy.

A pain management evaluation can help determine whether cryotherapy fits your specific condition, or whether another drug-free approach may serve you better.

Frequently asked questions

Is cryotherapy any different from just using an ice pack?
The exposure is far colder and much shorter, and it is delivered under supervision rather than left resting on the skin. An ice pack cools tissue slowly and locally across many minutes, while cryotherapy uses brief extreme cold to provoke a stronger response. Whether that difference produces better results for a particular condition is still debated in the research.

What is the difference between whole-body and localized cryotherapy?
Whole-body treatment exposes most of the body to extreme cold in a chamber for a few minutes, while localized treatment directs cold at a single joint or muscle group. Localized application is the more conventional choice for one specific painful area. Whole-body use is more often chosen for general recovery, and the evidence supporting it is less settled.

Is cryotherapy safe for someone with heart or circulation problems?
It needs clearance first. Extreme cold briefly raises blood pressure and heart rate, so unstable heart disease, poorly controlled hypertension, Raynaud’s phenomenon and cold urticaria are usually reasons to avoid it. Reduced sensation from neuropathy also matters, because cold injury becomes much harder to notice. A medical history review before a first session is standard practice.

Should cryotherapy be used right after exercise or later in the day?
Timing depends on the goal. Cold applied immediately after hard exercise can ease soreness, but some research suggests routinely cooling straight after strength training may blunt part of the training adaptation. When cryotherapy is being used for pain management rather than athletic recovery, sessions are usually arranged around the treatment schedule rather than around workouts.

posts.excerpt: Water-based therapy has long been used in physical rehabilitation, and for good reason. Reducing the effect of gravity on painful joints can make movement possible for patients who otherwise struggle on land. Why water works is discussed in the science of aqua therapy. Why water reduces stress on painful joints Buoyancy supports a large percentage […]
posts.content:
Water-based therapy has long been used in physical rehabilitation, and for good reason. Reducing the effect of gravity on painful joints can make movement possible for patients who otherwise struggle on land. Why water works is discussed in the science of aqua therapy.

Why water reduces stress on painful joints

Buoyancy supports a large percentage of body weight when a person is submerged, which takes pressure off the knees, hips, and spine. This allows some patients to move and stretch in ways that would be too painful on dry land.

Conditions that may benefit

Aqua-based rehabilitation is often used to support recovery from arthritis, post-surgical stiffness, and general chronic joint pain. It is typically used as part of a broader recovery or maintenance plan rather than a stand-alone treatment.

What a session generally involves

Sessions usually include a combination of gentle range-of-motion exercises and light resistance work in a warm pool, guided by a trained therapist. The water’s resistance can also help build strength gradually without the joint impact of traditional exercise.

How this fits into a complete pain management plan

Aqua therapy works best alongside other treatment, not instead of it. Many non-surgical pain programs are built around drug-free technology, shockwave therapy, EMTT, and Class IV laser therapy, to directly target the source of pain, and a care team can help coordinate complementary rehabilitation like aqua therapy where it fits your recovery plan.

If joint or back pain has made land-based exercise difficult, ask your provider whether a combined approach makes sense for your condition.

Frequently asked questions

How much weight does water actually take off a painful joint?
Enough to change what movement is possible. The deeper a person stands, the more load the water carries, so waist-deep water removes a meaningful share of body weight and chest-deep removes considerably more. Therapists use depth as a dial, starting deeper when a joint is very painful and working toward shallower water as tolerance improves.

Does exercising in water build real strength or only keep joints moving?
It can build strength, because water resists movement in every direction and that resistance increases the faster a limb is pushed against it. What water does not provide is impact loading, which bone and tendon also need to stay robust. That is why pool work is usually one stage of a program rather than the whole of it.

Can aqua therapy be done at a community pool or a gym pool?
Sometimes, if the water is warm enough and the depth suits the exercises, though many public pools are kept cool for lap swimming, which can make stiff joints tighten rather than relax. Early supervision also matters, since the exercises have to match the diagnosis. A therapist can often adapt a program for another pool once technique is established.

Can aqua therapy be combined with shockwave or laser treatment?
Usually yes, and the two are commonly scheduled around each other rather than treated as alternatives, since one targets the painful tissue directly while the other restores movement and strength. Sequencing within a day is what providers tend to watch, often keeping vigorous pool work away from the period right after a session when the area may be sore.

posts.excerpt: Fluoroscopic-guided injections are one of the more precise interventional options available to Brooklyn pain patients. Here is what the procedure actually involves. How fluoroscopy is used across pain procedures is covered in fluoroscopic-guided injections for pain relief. What fluoroscopy adds to an injection Fluoroscopy is a real-time X-ray imaging technique that lets a physician see […]
posts.content:
Fluoroscopic-guided injections are one of the more precise interventional options available to Brooklyn pain patients. Here is what the procedure actually involves. How fluoroscopy is used across pain procedures is covered in fluoroscopic-guided injections for pain relief.

What fluoroscopy adds to an injection

Fluoroscopy is a real-time X-ray imaging technique that lets a physician see exactly where the needle is positioned before delivering medication. This precision is meant to improve accuracy compared to a standard, unguided injection.

Conditions this technique may be used for

Fluoroscopy-guided injections are commonly used for spinal conditions, including irritated nerves and inflamed joints, where precise placement of medication can make a meaningful difference in the level of relief a patient experiences.

What to expect during the procedure

The procedure is done in a clinical setting, typically takes under an hour, and most patients are able to go home the same day. Mild soreness at the injection site in the days following is common.

Understanding realistic outcomes

Relief from these injections varies by patient and by condition, and is often temporary rather than permanent. They are frequently used as one part of a broader treatment plan that may also include drug-free options like shockwave or laser therapy.

A consultation with a pain management specialist can help determine whether a fluoroscopy-guided injection fits your specific diagnosis and treatment goals.

Frequently asked questions

Is the contrast dye used in these injections a problem for people with allergies?
It can be, so any previous reaction to contrast should be reported before scheduling. Options include performing the procedure without contrast, using a different agent, or premedicating with steroids and antihistamines. A shellfish allergy, despite the common belief, is not the same thing as a contrast reaction and is not treated as a reason to avoid the procedure.

What is the difference between a nerve block and a steroid injection?
A nerve block delivers anesthetic to interrupt signals from a specific nerve, often as much to identify the pain source as to treat it, while a steroid injection places anti-inflammatory medication near irritated tissue with the aim of lasting longer. Many procedures combine both, which is why a short numb period can come before any anti-inflammatory effect appears.

What does it mean if a guided injection helps for only a few weeks?
It is still useful information. Short-lived relief usually confirms the medication reached the right structure, which supports the diagnosis even though the effect faded. From there a provider may repeat the injection within safe limits, add rehabilitation to address what keeps irritating the area, or consider a longer-acting procedure aimed at the same target.

Is numbness or weakness in a leg normal after a spinal injection?
A temporary numb or heavy feeling in a limb is common, because local anesthetic reaches nearby nerves, and it typically wears off within hours. Standing and walking should be done carefully until normal sensation returns. Numbness or weakness that appears later, gets worse, or affects bladder or bowel control is not expected and needs urgent assessment.

posts.title: Perineural Injection Therapy (PIT) For Pain Brooklyn NYC
posts.excerpt: Perineural injection therapy, often referred to as PIT, is a treatment option some patients explore when chronic nerve-related pain hasn’t responded well to more conventional approaches. What Perineural Injection Therapy Involves PIT involves injecting a dilute dextrose solution just under the skin, near nerves in the area where pain is felt, rather than into the […]
posts.content:
Perineural injection therapy, often referred to as PIT, is a treatment option some patients explore when chronic nerve-related pain hasn’t responded well to more conventional approaches.

What Perineural Injection Therapy Involves

PIT involves injecting a dilute dextrose solution just under the skin, near nerves in the area where pain is felt, rather than into the joint or muscle itself. The theory behind the treatment is that chronically irritated peripheral nerves can become inflamed and overly sensitive, a state sometimes called neurogenic inflammation, and that the injections may help calm that irritation. The underlying nerve science is examined in PIT therapy and the peripheral nerve matrix.

It’s worth being direct that PIT is a newer, less established treatment compared to options like physical therapy or steroid injections, and the research base is still developing. Some patients and practitioners report meaningful relief, particularly for chronic, localized nerve-type pain, but results are not consistent or guaranteed, and larger, high-quality studies are still limited. That trade-off is discussed in shockwave as an alternative to surgery and steroids.

Conditions Sometimes Treated With PIT

Patients typically ask about PIT for chronic regional pain that hasn’t improved with other treatments, including certain cases of nerve-related back, neck, or joint pain. Because the evidence is still emerging, PIT is usually considered after more established treatments have been tried, not as a first-line option.

What a Session Feels Like

The injections are shallow, just under the skin, and most patients describe brief stinging at each injection point rather than significant pain. Sessions are generally well tolerated, and side effects such as temporary redness or soreness at the injection sites are uncommon and short-lived. A treatment plan usually involves multiple sessions rather than a single visit.

Is PIT Right for You?

Because PIT is still an evolving treatment, a thorough evaluation is important before starting, so your provider can talk through what’s realistic for your specific condition. Individual results vary, and PIT is not guaranteed to relieve pain.

If you’re in Brooklyn and want to discuss whether perineural injection therapy could be part of your treatment plan, a pain management provider can walk you through the options, including what the evidence does and doesn’t show.

Frequently asked questions

What kind of pain is PIT least likely to help?
Pain driven by clear structural damage. Where the main problem is an advanced arthritic joint, a significant tear, a compressed nerve root or an inflammatory disease, a superficial dextrose injection is not addressing the cause. It is aimed at irritation of small nerves near the surface, so the evaluation is largely about deciding whether that picture fits.

Can several sites along a nerve path be treated in one PIT session?
Often yes, since each site takes only a moment and the injections stay superficial. The practical limits are the total volume that is reasonable in one sitting, how much brief stinging a person wants to tolerate, and whether treating a long stretch at once makes it harder to judge what responded. A provider decides that case by case.

How is PIT different from a nerve block?
A nerve block uses anesthetic, sometimes with steroid, to interrupt signals from a specific nerve, often placed under image guidance. Perineural injection therapy instead puts dilute dextrose into the tissue just under the skin near the nerve, aiming to settle irritation rather than numb the area. Blocks are also used diagnostically, which is not the purpose of PIT.

Is a small bump or stinging at the injection sites normal after PIT?
Yes. A raised bump where the fluid sits under the skin is expected and settles within hours, and brief stinging during the injection is the sensation most people describe. Redness that spreads, increasing pain over the following days, or fever is a different matter and should be reported rather than waited out.

posts.title: Shockwave Therapy in Brooklyn: How It Works and What It Treats
posts.excerpt: TL;DR Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) sends acoustic pressure waves into painful tissue to trigger the body’s healing response. It is used for long-lasting tendon and soft tissue pain that has not improved with rest and exercise. The strongest evidence is for plantar fasciitis, calcific shoulder tendinitis and tennis elbow. Sessions take about 10 to 20 […]
posts.content:
TL;DR

Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) sends acoustic pressure waves into painful tissue to trigger the body’s healing response. It is used for long-lasting tendon and soft tissue pain that has not improved with rest and exercise.

  • The strongest evidence is for plantar fasciitis, calcific shoulder tendinitis and tennis elbow.
  • Sessions take about 10 to 20 minutes, with no needles, anesthesia or downtime.
  • Most courses are 3 to 6 sessions, about a week apart.
  • Improvement usually builds over several weeks after the course.

What is shockwave therapy?

Shockwave therapy is a non-invasive treatment that uses acoustic waves, not electricity, delivered through the skin by a handheld device. “Extracorporeal” means the waves are created outside the body. There are two main types: focused shockwave, which reaches deeper tissue, and radial pressure wave therapy, which spreads more widely near the surface.

How does shockwave therapy work?

The pressure waves are thought to:

  • Stimulate new blood vessel growth in the treated tissue
  • Trigger a healing response in tendons that have stalled
  • Help break down calcium deposits
  • Calm pain signals in the area

What conditions does shockwave therapy treat?

  • Plantar fasciitis and heel pain. See shockwave therapy for plantar fasciitis.
  • Calcific tendinitis of the shoulder
  • Tennis elbow and golfer’s elbow
  • Achilles tendinopathy
  • Patellar tendinopathy (jumper’s knee)
  • Outer hip pain (greater trochanteric pain syndrome)
  • Some cases of delayed bone healing

It is usually considered after at least a few months of other care, such as exercise and physical therapy.

What does the evidence say?

Large randomized trials have shown that focused shockwave therapy reduces heel pain in chronic plantar fasciitis more than placebo, and reduces pain and calcium deposits in calcific shoulder tendinitis. Evidence for other tendon problems is promising but more mixed. Shockwave is most effective alongside a strengthening program.

What does a session feel like?

  • A gel is applied and the device is placed on the painful area.
  • You feel tapping or pulsing that can be uncomfortable but is usually tolerable. The intensity can be adjusted.
  • A session takes about 10 to 20 minutes.
  • You can usually walk out and return to normal activity, avoiding heavy strain on the area for a day or two.
  • Mild soreness or redness for a day or two is common.

Who should not have shockwave therapy?

It is usually avoided:

  • During pregnancy
  • Over a cancer or an active infection
  • In people with bleeding disorders or on some blood thinners
  • Over open growth plates in children
  • Directly over the lungs, major nerves or blood vessels

Is shockwave therapy right for you?

It may fit if you have tendon or heel pain that has lasted more than three months and has not improved with rest, stretching and physical therapy. An evaluation confirms the diagnosis first, since some conditions respond better than others. Learn more about shockwave therapy at PainTherapyCare and how it compares in shockwave vs cortisone for tennis elbow.

Frequently asked questions

Does shockwave therapy hurt?

It can be uncomfortable, often described as strong tapping. The intensity can be adjusted to what you can tolerate.

How many shockwave sessions do I need?

Most courses are 3 to 6 sessions, about a week apart.

How long does it take to work?

Some people notice relief within a few weeks. Full improvement often builds over two to three months after the course.

Is shockwave therapy covered by insurance?

Coverage varies a lot by plan and condition. Check with your plan before starting.

Should I stop anti-inflammatory medicine during shockwave therapy?

Some providers suggest limiting it, since shockwave works partly by triggering a healing response. Talk to the prescriber before changing any medication.

Take the next step

If this sounds like what you are dealing with, you do not have to figure it out alone. A pain management provider can evaluate what is going on and walk you through drug-free, non-surgical options that may fit your situation.

Ready to get real relief?

We verify your coverage before your visit and build a non-surgical plan that fits you.

Book Your Appointment

J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2015;97(9):701-708; Gerdesmeyer L, et al. Extracorporeal shock wave therapy for the treatment of chronic calcifying tendonitis of the rotator cuff: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003;290(19):2573-2580.

posts.title: Physical And Occupational Therapy In Brooklyn, New York
posts.excerpt: Physical and occupational therapy remain two of the most established, evidence-based tools in pain management, and understanding the difference between them can help patients get more out of their treatment plan. What physical therapy focuses on Physical therapy generally focuses on restoring movement, strength, and function, often through targeted exercises, stretching, and manual techniques designed […]
posts.content:
Physical and occupational therapy remain two of the most established, evidence-based tools in pain management, and understanding the difference between them can help patients get more out of their treatment plan.

What physical therapy focuses on

Physical therapy generally focuses on restoring movement, strength, and function, often through targeted exercises, stretching, and manual techniques designed to address a specific injury or condition.

What occupational therapy focuses on

Occupational therapy focuses more on helping patients perform daily activities and tasks, adapting movement patterns or routines so patients can return to work, hobbies, and everyday life with less pain and greater independence.

How these therapies complement drug-free treatment

Physical and occupational therapy often work well alongside technology-based treatments like shockwave therapy, EMTT, and Class IV laser therapy, addressing both the underlying tissue and the functional movement patterns that surround an injury.

Building a complete recovery plan

Combining therapy with drug-free technology gives patients a more complete plan, one that addresses pain directly while also rebuilding the strength and habits needed to prevent it from returning.

If you are recovering from an injury or managing chronic pain, ask your Brooklyn pain management provider how physical or occupational therapy could fit into your broader treatment plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can physical therapy and occupational therapy happen at the same time?
Yes, and they often overlap by design. One side works on movement, strength and mobility, the other on performing daily tasks with less pain, so the two plans are normally coordinated rather than run in competition. Where scheduling limits how many visits are realistic, the therapists usually agree between them which focus comes first.

Is occupational therapy only for people going back to work?
No. Occupation here means any daily activity that matters to a person, from dressing and cooking to gardening, driving or lifting a grandchild. Returning to a job is one common goal, but occupational therapy is used just as often by retired people who want everyday tasks to be less painful and more manageable.

Should therapy come before or after treatments like shockwave or laser?
Often both, in sequence. Technology-based treatments are frequently timed to settle pain and prepare tissue so that strengthening and movement work can be tolerated, and the therapy that follows is what tends to make the gains hold. The order depends on the diagnosis and on how irritable the area is at the time.

Do home exercises between sessions actually matter?
They usually matter more than the sessions themselves. An hour a week in a clinic is a small share of the load a joint sees, and most therapy programs are built around what gets repeated at home. Saying honestly what is and is not being done at home lets the program be adjusted rather than quietly abandoned.

Physical therapy that did not get you all the way there?

A fresh evaluation looks at what was never tested. More on physical and occupational therapy.
